blocks.text: Letters Between Two Drops
Era Three · Epistolary adventure · Messages kept by a roof mender
1. Dema's work note
South gutter: three cracked joins. Catchment leaves need turning before the heavy rain. Do not scrape the green material beneath the second join until identified.
I added the last sentence after the material flashed at me.

I mend roofs in the City of Rainward Roofs. Usually a flashing gutter means somebody upstream has misconnected a message drum. This flash came from the underside of a moss stem, in a pattern too small and quick for my ordinary sight.
I brought my inspection lens close. An old slow-view setting stretched the bright movements into separate marks. Between one bead falling from the join and the next, the moss contained a street.
On that street someone was waving a square of white fiber.
I put down my scraper.
2. Issa to the shape above the channel
If you can distinguish this writing, remove your shadow from the south wall. We use its warmth to raise the carrier current. You have been standing over it through two loading shifts.
Thank you for not cleaning us.
I am Issa, pilot of the lower capillary. The white fiber is a notice, not a surrender. If you are a collector, we have nothing for sale that can survive the size of your hands.
If you are the roof keeper, we need to discuss the second join.
3. Dema to Issa
I am a roof mender. My name is Dema. I moved the lens so you should have warmth again.
I am writing by scratching a film of dark repair wax and letting the lens reduce it onto your fiber. Tell me if this hurts anything. I have never done it before.
The join will break during heavy rain. I was going to replace the strip below it. Your town appears to be attached to that strip.
How long do you need to move?
4. Issa to Dema
Your message reached us upside down. We held an argument over whether it was a threat before someone climbed onto the back of the fiber.
No one was injured by the writing. Three people were offended by the suggestion that we move a town. I was one of them. I have recovered enough to answer.

We call this place Between the Drops. We have streets in the leaf veins, store bubbles beneath the moss, and a nursery in the fork where your enormous crack seems narrowest. One falling drop occupies much of a journey for us. Your rain is a migration season.
We do not know how to translate “during heavy rain” into the number of journeys available.
Please describe what the water is doing, not when it will do it.
Also: move your smallest finger. It is closing the western road.
5. Dema's note to the watershed crew
Delay work at the south gutter. Occupied habitat confirmed beneath the second join. I am establishing a diversion and a receiving place with the inhabitants.
Do not mark the gutter abandoned if I stop answering the roof drum. The slow-view lens makes the intervals difficult to judge.
Please bring the narrow brace, not the scraping blade.
6. Dema to Issa
The pool above the join is now touching the blue stain. When it covers the stain, water will reach the broken edge. I can show you the stain through the lens.
I cannot stop the whole watershed. Three roofs send water here and one carries a healing house's clean supply. I can divide the flow if I fit a brace at the sound edge.
There is moss on the next strip, but I do not know whether it is a place you can live.
If you tell me what makes a place suitable, I can look.
7. Issa to Dema
I have examined your other moss. It has food life, but its lower film drains too quickly. The young would dry during the long bright intervals. We cannot simply be placed on something green.

There is a route behind the little light on our east wall. We have always used it to guide shallow-water boats. The lamp keeper says it belongs to a lighthouse with rooms inside its rooms. If your lens can follow the light, perhaps your larger side has an entrance too.
Do not turn the light up. A former keeper tried that. It made navigation easier for exactly the people who did not live under it.
I will investigate after I eat. I have been issuing instructions for two shifts and have become unpleasant.
My apprentice says I was unpleasant before the emergency.
8. Dema to Issa
I found a small tower inside the inspection recess. I would have mistaken it for a screw housing if you had not described the light.

Following the beam brought the entrance into view. Inside, the first landing held another tower. Its keeper could see a shape moving where my lens stood, but could not find an outer wall they trusted. I will not pull any of it apart.
The keeper can carry a signal between our scales. They cannot carry your whole village. They suggested matching a receiving water film before opening a route.
I have braced the damaged strip. It should hold while we try.
You asked what I eat. Usually something cold, standing up, because I tell myself the next roof will be the last.
Your apprentice may be right about you. Mine would be right about me, if I had one.
9. Issa to Dema
We made the journey through the east lamp. It took longer than expected. Each landing had a different keeper and every keeper believed they maintained the largest sensible scale.

The third keeper brought us to a reservoir lip in the next strip. There is enough sheltered water. There are hunters in the upper moss, which means we need a covered route and cannot move the nursery first.
We can build the route if you hold a fiber between the two sound edges. It must touch the films without draining one into the other. A bridge made too steep becomes a flood.
I enclose a drawing. The marks beside it show acceptable movement; they are not decoration.

I also enclose a story my apprentice tells about you: once there was a roof mender so large that rain could land on them without breaking their house. They were lonely because nobody could shout loudly enough to borrow their tools.
Is it accurate?
10. Dema's private note
The story is not accurate. I have neighbors. I have been avoiding one of them since we argued over a repair I promised and did not finish.
I ate while watching the slow-view lens. Issa's people completed half a covered bridge. By the time I washed my bowl they had dismantled it, moved the supports, and built something better.
I began to understand why my silences seemed careless to them.
I marked my messages AVAILABLE, AWAY, or RETURNING. Those were promises about what I intended to do, not claims that their time would wait for me.
Then I went to ask the neighbor for help.
11. Venn to Dema
Issa is asleep. I am the apprentice, Venn.

We received your fiber. You lowered it well. The landing shifted when the west runoff began, but we tied it before anyone crossed. Please keep the brace where it is even if it looks crooked from your side.
The blue stain is almost covered.
The nursery cannot use the first bridge because the water film is too thin along the center. We are threading a second fiber beside it. Their carriers will move between the two.
Issa would say this more politely: do not help by making the crossing smooth. We tied the knots where travelers can hold during a surge.
12. Dema to Venn and Issa
I see the knots. I will leave them.
The watershed crew can divert the first surge for one basin-filling interval. I do not know how long that is on your side. I have hung a marker in the basin so you can watch the change.
I am going to tighten the brace. You will feel three small movements. They are from my hand. Anything after the third is the strip itself moving.
If the strip breaks, I can catch it in a wet tray. That would keep it from falling, but I cannot promise its channels would remain intact. Move anyone who can travel now.
I am staying at the lens.
13. The crossing record
Three small movements.
Then a fourth.

The old strip began peeling from the gutter while its upper moss still held. Under the lens it resembled a cliff deciding, very slowly, to become a roof. Streets tilted. A store bubble burst, sweeping food and tools toward the broken edge.
Dema's neighbor held the catch tray. Dema kept the crossing fiber level. Neither could reach the torn strip without releasing something more necessary.
On the little bridge, carriers moved the nursery between parallel strands. One stopped at a knot and would not advance. A second carrier went back. The line buckled around them and held.
Dema watched the basin marker rise. They wanted to hurry the travelers with a shout. The lens showed how much of the crossing their smallest movement occupied. They kept still.
Issa's boat appeared beneath the fiber, collecting those swept off the old street. It made two crossings. On the third, the boat vanished behind a folded moss blade.
The basin filled.
Water crossed the blue stain and covered the join.
Dema and the neighbor caught the old strip together. The lens showed only bright turbulence.
14. Dema to Between the Drops
I have the strip in a wet tray. Its lower edge is torn. The brace held long enough to keep the bridge attached to the receiving side.
Please answer through the lamp if the fiber is gone.
Please tell me who arrived.
I will keep the tray shaded and the water still until you can inspect it.
15. Venn to Dema

The nursery arrived. Most households arrived. Some stores were lost. The western street broke after its last occupied house was cleared. We have not inspected every closed bubble in the torn strip, so do not dispose of it.
Issa's boat came through the lower film. One runner broke. Issa hurt a forelimb but is awake and complaining about the receiving harbor.
The place you helped us reach is not our old village. It has a sour smell at low water. We will have to move one shelter before the hunters return. We are arguing about its name.
We are here.
Issa says your drawing of the brace was terrible and saved us considerable time.
16. Issa to Dema
My forelimb is healing. Venn pilots the lower route now. I am trying to learn how to give advice without assuming that being injured has made me wise.

We inspected the caught strip. Two travelers were sheltering beneath a sealed root. They are home. You can return the remaining living moss to the damp recess; it still has inhabitants who never used our streets.
I have named my new boat Your Smallest Finger. Venn says that joke is already old. From your side, perhaps it has only just happened.

We cannot keep friendship by counting equal days. I propose this instead: send a description of one thing you noticed when you have time. I will answer with one thing from here. Neither message will oblige the other to remain unchanged until it arrives.
Today I noticed the sour harbor smells sweeter after the carriers pass.
17. Dema to Issa
Today my neighbor returned a tool and stayed to eat.
I told them your story about the giant who could not borrow anything. They said it was accurate in every respect except the size.

We fitted an inspection door above your lamp. It opens from our side without shading your south wall. Venn's current drawing is fixed inside it. There is a second space for the next drawing, because I have learned that a saved map can become a dangerous promise.
The gutter is repaired. Your crossing remains.
I am going home before the last roof is finished. Another mender has agreed to take it tomorrow.
18. A later letter from Venn

Issa no longer pilots, but still corrects my knots. They asked me to send the enclosed description of our harbor festival. I have left in the complaint about the music. They would notice if I removed it.
The children call the inspection door Dema's Sky. I tell them a person lives beyond it, among other people, with work and meals and neighbors. They prefer the idea that the sky has a name.
When your answer comes, some of them may already be apprentices. Address it to whoever is keeping the lamp. We will read it aloud to anyone who wishes to listen.
Issa says: the harbor is still sour. I like it now.
19. The note beneath the work order
Dema never settled on a reliable conversion between roof time and village time. They stopped treating this as unfinished arithmetic.

The repaired join required inspections, then a new brace, then a different kind of fiber when the old one wore. The village changed its name twice. The lighthouse keepers disagreed about the outermost scale. The rain came when it came.
Inside the inspection door, below the repair instructions, Dema kept one sentence in large writing:
Before replacing this part, ask who is using it.
Under that, small enough to need the lens, Venn had added:
Then wait for the answer.
